Tutorials (30)
Interface tour
▶ Show me
RackDroid Guide
The rack

RackDroid is a modular synthesizer: you place modules on a rack, connect them with cables, and everything makes sound in real time. The essentials are built in, with many more packs available on demand.
Getting around
Scroll the rack with one finger on the background, or two fingers anywhere. Pinch to zoom. View ▸ Zoom to fit modules frames your whole patch.
Adding modules

Open the palette with the 🧩 button in the tool row: the strip along the bottom shows the category chips and the module tiles. Use 🔍 to search by name, brand or tag, and tap a tile to place it. Hold a tile for 3 seconds for details.
Knobs and switches
Drag a knob up or down to turn it. Long-press a knob to open its menu and type an exact value.
Cables
Drag from any port to another port to create a cable. Drag a plug away to move or remove it. Outputs can feed many inputs.
Sound and recording
The Audio 2 module is already connected to your speakers — anything you patch into its TO inputs plays. Tap ⏺ to record the master output as WAV into Documents/RackDroid.
Keyboards and MIDI
⌨ opens an on-screen piano (add a MIDI to CV module to use it for pitch/gate). 🎹 scans for Bluetooth MIDI controllers; USB controllers also work.
Padlocks
🔒 freezes modules and cables in place while knobs stay live — great for performing. 🔐 freezes everything, parameters included. Two-finger navigation always works.
Saving and sharing
File ▸ Save stores your patch. File ▸ Share patch… sends the current patch as a .vcv file to any app. Opening a .vcv file from another app imports it.
Undo and language
↶ and ↷ undo and redo any change. The interface follows your phone\'s language; Help ▸ Language sets a different one.

Interface tour
Welcome to RackDroid
A full modular synth in your pocket. Here is a tour of the screen, piece by piece: what is there and what it does. You can skip it any time.
The toolbar

Up top: the menus (File, Edit, View, Engine, Help) and two rows of tools — module palette, module manager, cable parking, theme, MIDI, on-screen keyboard, record, info; below: undo/redo, multi-select, copy, paste, bin and the two padlocks. The ⌄ arrow folds it away.
Adding modules
The bar at the bottom is the module palette: tap a category chip or the 🔍 to search, then tap or drag a tile onto the rack. The ⓘ on a tile shows its name, description and tags.
Cable parking
On the left: park a cable end in a hole, scroll to the far module, then drag it out onto the port — compatible ports light up. It grows from 3 to 10 holes; the handle at the top collapses it.
The rack — gestures
Drag a module\'s panel to move it — watch this one slide across and come back. Long-press a knob to type an exact value; long-press a module for its own menu.
That\'s it
You start on a demo patch that already makes sound. To go deeper, open Help ▸ Guide and Help ▸ Tutorials (30 guided paths). Have fun!
The menus, up top
File opens, saves and shares patches. Edit holds undo and selection. View covers zoom, theme and how cables look. Engine is audio and sample rate. Help has the guide and the tutorials.
Building and playing
The first row of tools: the module palette, the pack manager, cable parking, the theme, MIDI devices, the on-screen keyboard, recording and information.
Editing
The second row: undo and redo, multi-select, copy, paste and the bin. These are what you reach for while tidying a patch.
The two padlocks
The first freezes modules and cables in place while knobs stay live: play a set without nudging anything by mistake. The second locks the parameters as well. Both survive between sessions.
More modules
This is where .rdmod packs are installed: dozens more modules, without updating the app. They appear in the palette straight away, and you can remove them from here too.
Choosing several modules

The multi-select button is lighting up now — watch. With it on, a tap picks a module and another tap drops it, and the chosen ones get a red halo. Hold one to move them all together, or use copy, paste and the bin beside it.
Sound, MIDI and recording

The on-screen keyboard plays without any other hardware; the MIDI button scans for Bluetooth controllers (USB ones work as soon as they are plugged in). The red dot records the output to a WAV file in your Documents folder.
The File menu
New patch, open and save, save a copy, overwrite the template you start from, import a selection, and share the patch with another app. The patches you opened recently are in here too.
The Edit menu

Undo and redo, select all or deselect. With modules chosen: copy, paste, duplicate them — with or without their cables — initialise or randomise them, disconnect their cables, bypass them, or delete them. Clear cables strips every cable in the patch.
The View menu

Frame rate, interface size, zoom to fit every module on screen, light or dark theme, tooltips, cable colours, how knobs respond, locked module positions — and the two sliders that set how tight and how visible the cables are.
The Engine menu
Performance meters, sample rate, and how many CPU threads the audio engine uses. Raise the rate for quality, lower it if a big patch starts to crackle.
The Help menu
Language, the guide by topic, the thirty tutorials — and this tour, which you can replay from here whenever you like.
Zoom and scrolling

Pinch with two fingers to zoom in and out, and drag the background with one finger — or two fingers anywhere — to scroll. Let go while still moving and the rack glides on. Watch it come closer, then slide across.
Patching
Drag from an output to an input: the cable follows your finger and every jack that can take it lights up, so you can aim roughly and still land it. Watch one being drawn.
If you want a hand
Help holds the topic guide and thirty step-by-step tutorials that build real patches, from your first sound to the advanced techniques. You can run this tour again from there whenever you like.
Welcome! Let\'s build your first sound in six short steps. You can keep using the rack while this card is open.
Open the module palette: tap the 🧩 button at the left of the tool row. The strip appears along the bottom of the screen.
Type VCO in the search box and tap the first tile. That places an oscillator — the source of your sound.
Now search for Audio and add "Audio 2" the same way (skip if it\'s already in the rack). It sends sound to your speakers.
Connect them: drag from the VCO\'s SAW output down at the bottom to a TO input on Audio 2. A cable appears.
You should hear a steady tone! Drag the VCO\'s FREQ knob up and down to change the pitch.
Use the LEVEL knob on Audio 2 for volume. To stop the sound, drag the plug away from the port.
Done! Save with File ▸ Save. The full guide is in Help ▸ Guide. Have fun!
Pro tutorial (30 steps)
Subtractive synth, explained
Welcome to the Pro tutorial! In 30 steps we\'ll build a complete synth voice — sequencer, oscillator, filter, envelope, amplifier, modulation — and explain WHY every cable goes where it goes.
The big idea: audio flows left to right (source ▸ tone shaping ▸ volume ▸ speakers), while CONTROL VOLTAGES (CV) automate knobs. Every cable carries one or the other.
Find some empty rack space (drag the background with one finger). We\'ll build there so nothing else gets in the way.
Add a VCO (palette 🧩, search VCO). The Voltage Controlled Oscillator generates the raw wave — it\'s the vibrating string of the synth. Alone it\'s just a steady buzz.
Look at its outputs: SIN is a pure tone, TRI is mellow, SAW is bright and rich in harmonics, SQR is hollow. We\'ll use SAW — all those harmonics give the filter something to carve.
Add a VCF. The Voltage Controlled Filter is the chisel: a low-pass filter lets lows through and cuts highs. Subtractive synthesis = start rich, carve away.
Connect VCO SAW ▸ VCF IN. Why: the raw wave must pass THROUGH the filter to be shaped. Audio chain, link one.
Listen in: connect VCF LOWPASS ▸ Audio 2 TO (temporarily). You\'ll hear a steady tone.
Drag the VCF\'s CUTOFF knob. Down = darker (harmonics removed), up = brighter. That knob is the single most expressive control on a synth.
Now RESONANCE: it boosts the band right at the cutoff. High values whistle — that\'s the classic \"acid\" character.
Problem: the tone never stops. Real notes start and end. For that we need a volume gate — a VCA — and something to drive it — an envelope.
Add a VCA. The Voltage Controlled Amplifier is a volume knob turned by voltage: no CV in, no sound out. That\'s exactly what we want — silence between notes.
Re-route: disconnect VCF LOWPASS from Audio 2 (drag the plug away) and connect VCF LOWPASS ▸ VCA IN instead. Why: volume control belongs AFTER tone shaping.
Connect VCA OUT ▸ Audio 2 TO. Chain complete: VCO ▸ VCF ▸ VCA ▸ speakers. It\'s silent now — the VCA is waiting for its control voltage.
Add an ADSR. It draws the volume shape of a note: Attack (fade-in time), Decay (fall after the peak), Sustain (held level), Release (fade-out after you let go).
Connect ADSR ENV ▸ VCA CV. Why: the envelope\'s curve becomes the note\'s loudness curve. Percussive or pad-like — it\'s all in these four knobs.
The ADSR needs to know WHEN a note happens: that\'s the GATE input. We could press a key… or let a sequencer play for us.
Add a SEQ 3. A step sequencer loops through steps, sending a voltage (the pitch) and a trigger (the rhythm) for each one. It\'s your robot performer.
Connect SEQ 3 TRIG ▸ ADSR GATE. Why: every step \"presses the key\" for you, firing one envelope per step.
Connect SEQ 3 CV (row 1) ▸ VCO V/OCT. Why: pitch in modular is a voltage — 1 volt = 1 octave. The row-1 knobs literally become your melody.
Press RUN on the SEQ 3. It cycles! If you hear nothing, raise the ADSR\'s SUSTAIN and shorten ATTACK.
Tune the melody: drag the row-1 CV knobs — each one is a step\'s note. TEMPO sets the speed, STEPS how many before the loop restarts.
Shape the groove on the ADSR: short Attack + short Decay + low Sustain = plucky; long Attack + high Sustain = pad. Try both.
Time for motion. Add an LFO — an oscillator too slow to hear, used as a CV. Its whole job is wiggling other modules\' knobs for you.
Connect LFO TRI ▸ VCF CUTOFF (the CV input next to the knob). Why: the cutoff now sweeps up and down by itself — the classic wobble.
Control the depth: the small knob beside the VCF\'s CUTOFF CV input scales how much the LFO moves it. CV inputs almost always have one — attenuators are your friends.
The LFO\'s FREQ sets wobble speed. Slow = tide, fast = growl. Notice you\'re now \"playing\" three modules at once without touching the audio path.
Experiment: move the LFO cable from VCF CUTOFF to VCO FM — now it wiggles PITCH (vibrato) instead of brightness. Same CV, different destination, different effect. That\'s the whole modular idea.
Add a Scope and connect VCA OUT ▸ Scope IN. Watch the waveform breathe as you tweak: seeing the envelope and the filter at work makes everything click.
Done — a full subtractive voice! Save it (File ▸ Save), share it (File ▸ Share patch…). Next ideas: a second detuned VCO into the same VCF, or swap the VCO for Macro Oscillator 2. Have fun!
Getting started
The rack, gestures, saving — all the basics
Finding modules
Search, filters, favorites, module info
The browser
Open it with the 🧩 button in the tool row. Tap 🔍 to search: type part of a name, brand or tag; the chips filter by brand (white = active) and by function. Installed expansion packs show up here too.
Tiles

Tap a tile to place the module where you long-pressed. Hold a tile for 3 seconds for its description, tags and license. Tap the ☆ on a tile to mark a favorite, then use the ★ Favorites chip to see only those.
Managing modules on the rack
Drag a module by its panel to move it. Long-press a module to open its context menu: presets, randomize, duplicate, delete. ↶ undoes anything.
Working on several modules

The multi-select button (the dashed frame in the tool row) changes what one finger does: while it is on, a tap on a module adds it to the selection and another tap removes it — knobs and jacks stay put, so you cannot nudge a value while choosing. Selected modules get a red halo and the panel stays readable. Holding one of them moves them all together, cables following; dragging from empty rack draws the usual selection box, and a tap on empty rack clears everything. With modules selected: copy and paste duplicate them wherever you like, and the bin deletes them, asking first and telling you how many are going.
Cables and signals
Audio vs CV, V/Oct, gates and triggers
Two kinds of signal, one kind of cable
Everything is a voltage. AUDIO signals (roughly ±5V) are what you hear; CONTROL VOLTAGES (CV) move parameters instead. Any output can drive any input — that freedom is the point of modular.
Pitch and rhythm conventions
Pitch: 1 volt = 1 octave (the V/OCT inputs). Rhythm: a GATE is high while a note is held; a TRIGGER is a short pulse that fires an event — envelopes, drums, sequencer steps.
Patching
Drag from a port to a port to connect. Drag a plug away to move or remove the cable. One output can feed many inputs; an input accepts one cable.
Cable colors
View ▸ Cable colors lets you set the rotation of colors — handy to tell pitch, gate and audio runs apart in a dense patch.
Cable parking

Two modules never fit on screen at once? Use the parking bar on the left (the cable-parking toolbar button toggles it; it is on at start). Drop a cable end into a hole, scroll to the far module, then drag it back out — compatible ports light up so you can aim. It starts with 3 holes and grows up to 10 as you fill them. Drop a pulled-out end in empty space to discard it; the chevron at the top collapses the bar to a handle.
Oscillators
VCO vs LFO, waveforms, detune and FM
VCO and LFO
Both make waves. A VCO runs at audio rate — you hear it. An LFO runs below hearing range — you use it as CV to move knobs (vibrato, wobble, tremolo).
Waveforms
SIN: pure, no harmonics. TRI: soft. SAW: bright, every harmonic — the filter\'s favorite food. SQR: hollow, odd harmonics only; its PW (pulse width) changes the color.
Fat sounds
Two VCOs on the same V/OCT, one slightly detuned (FINE knob): instant width. FM input: modulate pitch with an LFO for vibrato, or with another VCO at audio rate for metallic timbres.
Filters
Cutoff, resonance, and where they sit
The chisel
A filter removes harmonics. LOWPASS keeps lows (the classic synth sound); HIGHPASS keeps highs (thin, telephone-like). CUTOFF sets where the cut begins.
Resonance and drive
RESONANCE boosts the band at the cutoff: from subtle emphasis to whistling self-oscillation. DRIVE pushes the input harder for saturation and grit.
Placement and movement
The filter sits between source and VCA: VCO ▸ VCF ▸ VCA. Its magic is movement — patch an LFO or an envelope into the CUTOFF CV input and dose it with the little attenuator knob.
Envelopes and dynamics
ADSR, VCA, plucks and pads
Why notes need envelopes
Oscillators never stop. The VCA is a voltage-controlled volume knob (silent by default); the ADSR draws the shape that opens and closes it for every note.
The four stages
Attack: fade-in time. Decay: fall after the peak. Sustain: the held LEVEL (not a time!). Release: fade-out after the gate ends. The GATE input starts and ends the cycle.
Recipes
Pluck: A=0, short D, S=0. Pad: long A, high S, long R. Send the same envelope to the filter\'s CUTOFF CV as well and brightness follows loudness — very natural.
Drums
The RackDroid Drums voices, triggering, mixing
The pack
RackDroid Drums has 14 analog-style voices: 808 (deep, round), 909 (punchy, clicky), 606 (thin, boxy), 707 (mid-forward) and a 505 tom. All synthesized, all tunable.
Triggering

Every voice fires on a TRIG pulse — from a sequencer\'s gate/trig outputs, a MIDI drum pad, or gate modules. The hi-hats have CH and OH inputs: the closed hat chokes the open one, like the real machines.
Shaping and mixing
TUNE and DECAY reshape each voice a lot — an 808 kick with long decay is a bassline. Sum the voices with a mixer (e.g. VCA Mix) before Audio, and leave headroom: drums peak hard.
MIDI and keyboards
On-screen keys, Bluetooth and USB controllers
MIDI to CV
Modular speaks voltages, controllers speak MIDI. The MIDI to CV module translates: V/OCT for pitch, GATE for key-down, plus velocity, mod wheel and pitch bend outputs.
Connecting controllers
🎹 in the toolbar scans for Bluetooth MIDI devices. USB controllers plugged via OTG appear as MIDI devices too. Pick the device inside the MIDI to CV panel display.
The on-screen keyboard
⌨ opens a piano strip that sends MIDI to the same MIDI to CV module — perfect for testing a patch without hardware.
Mixing and recording
Levels, WAV recording, sharing patches
Getting to the speakers
Audio 2\'s TO inputs are your master bus; its LEVEL knob is the final volume. With several voices, sum them in a mixer (VCA Mix) first and balance there.
Recording
⏺ in the toolbar records the master output as a WAV into Documents/RackDroid — tap again to stop. What you hear is what you get.
Sharing and importing
File ▸ Share patch… sends the current patch as a .vcv to any app. Opening a .vcv from another app imports it (File ▸ Open to load it). Long-press a file in File ▸ Open to share it.
Performance and live use
Padlocks, engine settings, battery
Padlocks on stage
🔒 freezes module positions and cables but keeps knobs live — tweak without fear of dragging a module. 🔐 freezes everything for hands-off playback. Both persist across sessions.
Engine settings
Engine ▸ Threads spreads big patches over CPU cores. Engine ▸ Sample rate trades quality for headroom. Performance meters show each module\'s cost — find the heavy one.
Battery and heat
View ▸ Frame rate lowers UI redraws (audio is unaffected). Smaller patches, fewer reverbs and lower frame rates all run cooler on long sessions.
Tutorials
%1$d steps
Your first sound, step by step
The full subtractive voice, explained
Level 1 — Foundations
Level 2 — Modulation
Level 3 — Rhythm and sequencing
Level 4 — Effects
Level 5 — Advanced voices
Mixing two sources
Two VCOs into VC Mixer, balanced
We’ll blend two sounds into one output. Add a VC Mixer: four channels with level knobs and a master.
Add two VCOs (or reuse ones you have). Give them different pitches with their FREQ knobs.
Connect VCO 1 SAW ▸ mixer CH 1, and VCO 2 SAW ▸ CH 2.
Connect the mixer MIX output ▸ Audio 2 TO.
Balance with the CH 1 and CH 2 knobs; the big knob is the master volume.
Every patch with more than one voice ends in a mixer — it’s the mixing desk of your rack.
Seeing signals with Scope
Watch waves, envelopes and LFOs
The Scope draws voltages over time — the fastest way to UNDERSTAND what a module does. Add one.
Connect a VCO SAW ▸ Scope IN 1. There’s the sawtooth, tooth by tooth.
Turn the VCO FREQ down very low: watch the wave slow until you can follow it.
Now patch an LFO TRI ▸ IN 2: two signals at once. The TIME knob zooms in and out.
Habit to build: when something sounds wrong, scope it — you’ll SEE the problem.
Save, template, share
Never lose a patch again
File ▸ Save stores the patch; Save as gives it a name. The autosave also protects you from crashes.
File ▸ Overwrite template makes the CURRENT patch your File ▸ New starting point. Build your ideal default rack once.
File ▸ Share patch… sends the current patch as a .vcv file to any app — chat, mail, drive.
Receiving one? Open the .vcv from the other app and it lands in File ▸ Open.
In File ▸ Open, long-press any saved patch to share it directly.
Vibrato
A slow LFO wiggling the pitch
Vibrato = pitch gently wobbling. We need a VCO making sound (patch SAW ▸ Audio 2 if needed).
Add an LFO. Its TRI output is a smooth up-and-down voltage — perfect for vibrato.
Connect LFO TRI ▸ VCO FM. The FM input adds the LFO to the pitch.
Too much! Turn the VCO’s FM attenuator (small knob) way down: vibrato is subtle, ±20 cents.
Set the LFO FREQ around 5–6 Hz — the speed of a violinist’s hand.
Golden rule: modulation depth (attenuator) and speed (LFO rate) are two different controls. Learn to reach for the right one.
Tremolo
LFO on the VCA: pulsing volume
Tremolo = volume pulsing. Chain a voice through a VCA: source ▸ VCA IN, VCA OUT ▸ Audio 2.
Add an LFO and connect its TRI ▸ VCA CV.
Nothing? An LFO swings negative too: the VCA closes half the time. Raise the VCA LEVEL and lower the LFO amount for a gentler pulse.
LFO FREQ sets the character: 2 Hz is a slow wave, 8 Hz a flutter.
Try the SQR output instead of TRI: hard on/off gating — a completely different effect from the same module.
PWM: living squares
Pulse width modulation, the classic shimmer
Listen to a VCO’s SQR output: hollow and static. We’ll bring it alive.
The PW knob changes the square’s shape from thin pulse to fat square. Hear the color shift.
Now automate it: LFO TRI ▸ VCO PW input.
Slow LFO (0.5 Hz), moderate depth: the classic PWM shimmer — one oscillator that sounds like two.
PWM + filter + envelope is 80% of classic synth pads. You now own the trick.
Auto filter sweep
LFO on the cutoff, dosed right
Run a SAW through a VCF into Audio (VCO SAW ▸ VCF IN, LOWPASS ▸ Audio 2).
Patch LFO TRI ▸ VCF CUTOFF CV.
Use the attenuator beside the CUTOFF CV input to set sweep width, and the CUTOFF knob for the center.
Add RESONANCE: the sweep starts to sing.
Swap the LFO wave: TRI breathes, SQR chops, SAW ramps. Same patch, three effects.
Sample & Hold
Random voltages, stepped like R2-D2
S&H takes a snapshot of a signal at every trigger: from noise it makes random steps. Add Noise and S&H (SHASR).
Connect Noise WHITE ▸ S&H IN.
Add an LFO; its SQR ▸ S&H TRIG is the snapshot clock.
Send S&H OUT ▸ VCO V/OCT, with the VCO audible.
Random melody! LFO FREQ sets the tempo of the madness.
It’s chaos for now — the next tutorial tames it into a scale.
Quantizer: chaos to music
Snap any CV to a scale
A quantizer rounds any voltage to the nearest allowed note. Add one.
Insert it in the S&H line: S&H OUT ▸ Quantizer IN, Quantizer OUT ▸ VCO V/OCT.
On the quantizer’s little keyboard, disable notes until only a scale remains (try a minor pentatonic).
Same random source — now it’s music. This is THE trick behind generative patches.
Quantize anything: LFOs become arpeggios, envelopes become glissandi in key.
First 808 beat
Kick and snare from the sequencer
Add BD-808 and SD-808, and a SEQ 3 as the brain.
Each SEQ 3 step has its own STEP output at the bottom (the TRIG next to them is a different thing: it fires on whichever step is active). STEP outs 1 and 5 ▸ BD-808 TRIG (kick on the downbeats).
Step outs 3 and 7 ▸ SD-808 TRIG: the backbeat.
Mix both AUDIO outs into a mixer ▸ Audio 2, then press RUN.
Boom–clap! TEMPO sets the speed. Welcome to drum programming.
Tune the drums: BD TUNE/DECAY make it huge; SD SNAPPY adds crack.
Hi-hat groove
Closed chokes open, like the real thing
Add HH-808. It has TWO trigger inputs: CH (closed) and OH (open) — one voice, two articulations.
From SEQ 3, patch the even step outs ▸ CH: straight eighth notes.
Move ONE of them to OH instead: that step rings open.
Hear the choke: the next closed hit cuts the open tail — the classic “tss-t”.
O.DECAY sets how long the open hat rings. Longer = lazier groove.
Mix it under kick and snare — hats sit QUIETER than you think.
Acid bassline
SEQ3 CV into a squelchy filter
The recipe: SEQ 3 ▸ VCO ▸ VCF (high resonance) ▸ VCA ▸ Audio.
SEQ 3 CV row 1 ▸ VCO V/OCT; SEQ 3 TRIG ▸ ADSR GATE; ADSR ENV ▸ VCA CV.
Keep notes LOW: bass lives below 200 Hz. Program a simple loop with the row-1 knobs.
Now the acid: RESONANCE up high, CUTOFF low, and ADSR ENV also ▸ VCF CUTOFF CV.
Short envelope (A=0, D short): every note goes “mwip”. Sweep CUTOFF while it plays — that’s the 303 magic.
Small TEMPO and TUNE changes completely change the groove. Play with it — this patch rewards tweaking.
An LFO as clock
Square waves drive sequencers
Any square wave is a clock. LFO SQR ▸ SEQ 3 CLOCK input.
Now the LFO FREQ is your tempo — and it accepts CV, so tempo itself can be modulated…
Two sequencers from ONE clock stay locked together forever. That’s why external clocks matter.
The SEQ 3 RESET input restarts the pattern: patch a slower LFO SQR there for phrase-length loops.
Rule of thumb: one master clock per patch, everything else follows it.
Pattern variations
STEPS and RESET, fills for free
A running SEQ 3 loop gets boring. The STEPS knob changes the loop length live: try 6 instead of 8.
Odd lengths (5, 7) against 4/4 drums create rolling polyrhythms — instant interest.
The RESET input yanks the pattern back to step 1. Patch a slow LFO SQR there.
Now the phrase restarts every few bars — a free “arrangement”.
Live trick: twist STEPS for a moment and back — an instant fill.
Full 909 kit
Kick, snare, hats and a cowbell, mixed
Add BD-909, SD-909, HH-909 and CB-707: a full kit, brighter and punchier than the 808.
Distribute SEQ 3 step outs: kick on 1/5, snare on 3/7, hats on the evens, cowbell wherever it makes you smile.
All AUDIO outs ▸ mixer channels ▸ Audio 2. One knob per drum.
Balance: kick loudest, snare just under, hats way down, cowbell to taste.
PUNCH on the BD-909 and TONE on the SD-909 are the character knobs — sculpt your kit.
Record it: ⏺ in the toolbar captures your beat as WAV.
From here: swap voices for their 808/606 cousins and hear the eras change.
Echo
The Delay module, from slapback to dub
Insert a Delay AFTER your voice: source ▸ Delay IN, Delay OUT ▸ Audio 2.
TIME sets the gap between repeats, FDBK how many repeats, MIX the dry/wet blend.
Slapback: TIME ~80 ms, low feedback — instant rockabilly space.
Dub: long TIME, high feedback, and ride the knobs WHILE it repeats.
Feedback near max self-oscillates into infinite loops — an instrument in itself.
Delay on drums (just the snare send!) is a mixing classic.
Fake reverb from a delay
Dense echoes sound like a room
Real reverb needs an extra pack, but a Delay set to dense short echoes fakes a lush space. Add a Delay after your voice (voice ▸ Delay IN, Delay OUT ▸ Audio 2).
Set TIME very short (~60–100 ms) and FDBK high: the repeats blur into a wash the ear reads as a room.
MIX is dry/wet: low for a subtle tail, high for a cavern.
Add a SECOND Delay after the first with a slightly different TIME: the two dense trails overlap into a smoother, richer reverb.
Want a real plate/spring reverb? Install the Valley or Befaco pack (.rdmod, Modules folder). But now you know reverb is just clever echoes.
Flanger from a delay
A very short modulated delay
A flanger is a VERY short delay (1–10 ms) whose time wobbles, mixed with the dry — the classic jet-plane sweep. Add a Delay: voice ▸ IN, OUT ▸ Audio, MIX 50%.
TIME as short as it goes. LFO TRI ▸ Delay TIME CV, small depth, slow rate (0.3 Hz).
The comb notches sweep up and down: a metallic whoosh.
Raise FDBK for a sharper, more resonant flange — full airplane territory.
Chorus (next idea) and flanger are the same trick at different delay times. You now own both.
Chorus from a delay
Short modulated delay = width
Chorus is a ~20 ms delay whose time wobbles. Patch voice ▸ Delay, TIME very short, MIX 50%.
LFO TRI ▸ Delay TIME CV, depth low, rate slow (0.3 Hz).
The pitch wobbles slightly against the dry: that beating IS the chorus.
More depth → seasick vibrato-tape; faster → underwater. Find your spot.
You just built an EFFECT from raw parts — that’s the modular super-power.
Feedback adds flanger territory. Explore the edge.
Drive and distortion
Heat from the filter’s DRIVE
The VCF’s DRIVE pushes the signal into saturation before filtering. Voice ▸ VCF, raise DRIVE.
Compensate volume down at the VCA — distortion gets loud fast.
Sweep CUTOFF with high drive: the harmonics scream where a clean filter whispers.
On the 808 kick, drive = instant techno weight.
Saturation before the filter and after it sound DIFFERENT. Try both orders.
Stereo motion
Auto-pan with two VCAs and 8vert
Audio 2’s TO 1/TO 2 are LEFT and RIGHT. Split your voice into two VCAs: one per side.
LFO TRI ▸ VCA-left CV.
Add 8vert (a CV inverter): same LFO ▸ 8vert, its knob at −1, output ▸ VCA-right CV.
When the left opens, the right closes: the sound flies between your ears.
Slow LFO = gentle drift; audio-rate = rotary madness.
8vert flips ANY CV — one of the humblest, most useful modules in the case.
Sidechain ducking
The pad breathes with the kick
The pumping EDM effect: everything ducks when the kick hits. Route a pad/voice through a VCA.
Patch the kick’s trigger ALSO to an ADSR GATE (A=0, D~150 ms, S=0).
Invert it with 8vert (knob at −1) and into the VCA CV. Raise the VCA base LEVEL.
Every kick now pushes the pad down; it swells back between hits.
Deeper D = longer duck. That “breathing” is half of modern dance music.
Same trick on the hats or the reverb return = a mix that grooves by itself.
Two detuned VCOs
The oldest fattening trick
Two VCOs, same V/OCT source (mult the cable or stack from the output).
Both SAWs into a mixer, then filter → VCA as usual.
Detune VCO 2 with FINE, just a hair: the beating between them is the fatness.
Too much detune = honky-tonk; too little = flanging. The sweet spot breathes slowly.
Add Octave before VCO 2’s V/OCT to shift it −1 octave: instant sub-bass layer.
This is “supersaw” thinking with just two oscillators. Stack more if the CPU smiles.
Audio-rate FM
Bells and metal from two sines
FM at LFO speed is vibrato; at AUDIO speed it creates new harmonics. Two VCOs: carrier (heard) and modulator (not).
Carrier SIN ▸ Audio. Modulator SIN ▸ carrier FM. Raise the FM attenuator slowly.
The tone grows sidebands: clangs, bells, metal. The RATIO of the two pitches decides the flavor.
Tune the modulator to a harmonic ratio (octave, fifth): musical bells. Detune it: inharmonic gongs.
Envelope on the FM amount (via a VCA in the modulation path) = strike-then-mellow, like a real bell.
Congratulations — that’s the heart of the DX7, patched by hand.
Hard sync
Sync one VCO to another
Hard sync forces one oscillator to restart every cycle of another — aggressive, vowel-like timbres. Add two VCOs.
VCO 1 (the master) SQR ▸ VCO 2 SYNC. VCO 2 is the one you HEAR: VCO 2 ▸ Audio (via filter/VCA if you like).
VCO 1 sets the note you play: sequence or key its V/OCT.
Now sweep VCO 2 FREQ: the timbre morphs and screams while the pitch stays put — that\'s the sync sound.
Modulate VCO 2 FREQ with an LFO or envelope for the classic sync-sweep lead.
Sequence VCO 1\'s pitch to play a melody while VCO 2 sweeps: an instant expressive lead.
Plucked string (Karplus–Strong)
A string from noise + delay
Build a plucked string from scratch: a burst of noise trapped in a short delay loop. Add Noise and a Delay.
Noise ▸ Delay IN; Delay OUT ▸ Audio. (We\'ll shorten the noise to a burst next.)
Set Delay TIME very short — the delay length sets the PITCH (shorter = higher). FDBK high so it rings.
Put a low-pass VCF in the loop (Delay OUT ▸ VCF ▸ back in) so each repeat is darker — that\'s the string decaying.
Pluck it: gate the noise with a VCA + short envelope so only a brief burst enters — each trigger plucks the string.
Feed a drum trigger or sequencer gate to pluck rhythmically: rhythm becomes melody.
Generative patch
It plays itself
A generative patch makes music without you touching it. Build a basic voice (VCO ▸ VCF ▸ VCA ▸ Audio) or reuse one.
Add an LFO and a Sample & Hold (SHASR). A slow LFO SQR clocks the S&H; feed its IN from another LFO (or Noise).
Add a Quantizer: S&H OUT ▸ Quantizer ▸ VCO V/OCT — random-but-in-key notes on every clock. Disable notes to pick a scale.
A second slow LFO ▸ VCF CUTOFF so the timbre drifts on its own.
Add drums clocked by the same LFO for evolving rhythm — no two bars the same.
Lock the patch (🔒), press play, and just listen. Change ONE knob every minute.
Ambient drone
Slow everything, echoes for space
Recipe: two detuned VCOs ▸ filter ▸ VCA ▸ a dense Delay (our fake reverb) ▸ Audio. No sequencer.
Very slow LFO (0.05 Hz!) ▸ CUTOFF CV, tiny amount: the tone changes over MINUTES.
A second slow LFO ▸ VCO 2 FM (hair-thin): the beating drifts.
The Delay: short TIME, very high FDBK, generous MIX — dense echoes become an endless wash (see the fake-reverb tutorial).
Lock the patch (🔒), lower the lights, let it run. Every few minutes, ONE knob, ONE millimeter.
Record 10 minutes (⏺). Somewhere in there is your album intro.
Drone teaches the deepest lesson: modular is about listening, not playing.
